description: BNB Smart Chain smart contract publicly reported by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)/Mandiant as used by DPRK actor UNC5342 to host a second-stage JADESNOW payload retrieved via EtherHiding. A JavaScript downloader queries this contract's stored data via chain RPC calls to fetch and execute the payload, giving the actor a takedown-resistant hosting layer. This site read the contract directly on 2026-09-03 and reconstructed its write history from archive state, which no indexer covers because the contract emits no events. It was deployed 2025-02-07T04:47:45Z and its stored payload was rewritten 23 times through 2025-05-30, every write sent by the watchlisted owner address to selector 0xd3fc9864. The payload at deployment was 2,520 bytes that base64-decode to 1,890 bytes of readable obfuscated JavaScript; the payload it has served unchanged since 2025-05-30 is 5,216 bytes decoding to 3,909 bytes at 6.64 bits of entropy per byte, so encoded rather than readable. Between those two the payload swung between full multi-kilobyte scripts and short strings as brief as 28 bytes, so the contract was not only rotated but repurposed. The contract also carries the token-shaped cover strings "BOT250205" and "BOT", a name whose digits match its deployment week.

description: Ethereum wallet hard-coded into trojanized npm packages reported by OpenSourceMalware as part of the DPRK Contagious Interview campaign. The malware does not read a payload from it. It looks up the wallet's most recent outbound transaction and takes that transaction's destination address, decoding a command-and-control IP out of the address bytes. OpenSourceMalware attributes the activity to the DPRK Contagious Interview campaign and names no UNC cluster, so no UNC5342 attribution is asserted here. The packages named in that reporting are bianira-ui and fluid-type-ui, with five further packages added in a later update. This site enumerated all 285 outbound transactions from this wallet on 2026-09-03 and found the resolved destination rotated three times: 166.88.134.62 from 2026-07-25 to 2026-08-22 across 178 transactions, 23.27.13.135 from 2026-08-22 to 2026-08-27 across 48, and 166.88.73.46 from 2026-08-28 to 2026-09-03 across 58. Only the first appears in the cited reporting; the other two are recorded here from chain data.

Decoding it byte by byte reproduces exactly what the reporting describes: bytes 0-3 and bytes 4-7 both read as 166.88.134.62, and the trailing twelve bytes are the ASCII string "helloipbot!!". description: Ethereum wallet whose outbound transactions the September 2026 XCTDH implant scans for. A module the malware calls _Z samples recent blocks through public RPC endpoints, looks for transactions whose sender contains 33ff3edaf55a8e03dcbc7cb40d498a49, and decodes an IPv4 address and port from the first six bytes of the recipient address, the same recipient-address encoding OpenSourceMalware published as NullReceiver. Ransom-ISAC reports 2,655 outbound transactions from 23 June 2026 to 21 September 2026, one about every 50 minutes, with the encoded address rotated four times in that window, and calls the technique Hash Hiding. Ransom-ISAC labels the campaign DPRK-attributed and ties it to the same BSC wallet as its October 2025 series.

description: A second EtherRAT resolver contract of the same getString(address) / setString(string) design (selectors 0x7d434425 and 0x7fcaf666). The DFIR Report lists it and its operator wallet among the indicators of an April 2026 intrusion in which EtherRAT's configuration on Ethereum was repeatedly rewritten to point at TryCloudflare tunnels. This site read its write history on 3 October 2026: the operator wrote 31 values between 24 April and 1 October 2026, alternating TryCloudflare tunnels with parked values naming well-known domains, so a new value here is reviewed before it is treated as an indicator. The DFIR Report published this deployment as EtherRAT in an intrusion that ended in The Gentlemen ransomware and names no nation-state; the DPRK label rests only on Sysdig's attribution of the EtherRAT family, so this entry carries low confidence and should not be read as a DPRK attribution of the intrusion itself.
